content: Gingivitis, or inflammation of the gums, is a condition caused by bacterial biofilms, commonly referred to as plaque, that adhere to the surfaces of teeth. This condition is characterized by localized, reversible inflammation of the gingiva without any detectable loss of bone or connective tissue attachment. It is prevalent across all age groups, from children to adults, and is frequently observed during dental examinations. The development of gingivitis is multifactorial, often involving a combination of poor oral hygiene, genetic predisposition, socioeconomic and demographic factors, iatrogenic causes, and behavioral influences. These factors can complicate the identification of specific risk contributors. The condition begins with the accumulation of microbial plaque near the gingival sulcus. Other local and systemic factors may either promote plaque retention or increase the gingival tissue's susceptibility to bacterial attack. This leads to an inflammatory response, which initially presents as swelling (edema) and may progress to a more fibrotic state if left untreated. The earliest clinical sign of gingivitis is the transudation of gingival fluid, which evolves into a fluid containing serum and white blood cells. The redness of the gingival margin is due to the enlargement of blood vessels in the connective tissue beneath the epithelium and a loss of keratinization on the gingival surface. Despite these changes, gingivitis is often painless and rarely causes spontaneous bleeding, making it difficult for patients to recognize the condition. However, it is clinically significant as it is considered a precursor to periodontitis, a more severe condition involving connective tissue and bone loss. Gingivitis is reversible, and treatment focuses on controlling the causative factors to reduce inflammation and restore gingival health. Simple cases of gingivitis can be managed with proper oral hygiene practices, such as brushing and flossing, and the use of antibacterial mouth rinses. Professional cleaning, including scaling with hand or ultrasonic instruments, is also effective. Classification The classification of gingival diseases has evolved over time. In 2017, the American Academy of Periodontology and the European Federation of Periodontology updated the classification system during the World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-implant Diseases and Conditions. Gingivitis is diagnosed based on the presence of gingival inflammation at one or more sites and bleeding on probing. Stages Gingivitis progresses through four stages, as described by Page and Schroeder in 1976. If left untreated, it can advance to periodontitis. Pathophysiology Gingivitis originates from bacterial plaque that accumulates between the teeth and gums. If teeth are not adequately cleaned, the plaque mineralizes into calculus (tartar), which harbors bacteria and irritates the gingiva. As the plaque biofilm thickens, it creates an oxygen-deprived environment that promotes the growth of pathogenic bacteria, which release toxins and trigger inflammation. Vigorous brushing can also cause gum injury, leading to a cycle of recession, inflammation, and infection. In some cases, weakened immune defenses due to local or systemic conditions can exacerbate the infection. Over time, this inflammation can lead to the formation of deep pockets between the teeth and gums, as well as bone loss, progressing to periodontitis. Local Factors Crowded or misaligned teeth make plaque removal more difficult. Poorly fitted dental prostheses can act as a site for plaque accumulation. In children, tooth eruption can lead to eruptive gingivitis due to increased plaque in areas where primary teeth are exfoliating or permanent teeth are erupting. Infectious Gingivitis Local tissue injuries, such as fractured teeth or poorly designed dental restorations, can predispose individuals to gingivitis. Hypersensitive Reactions Allergens in products like chewing gum, toothpaste, or certain foods can trigger plasma cell gingivitis. Nutritional Gingivitis Diets high in refined carbohydrates and an imbalanced ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids can activate inflammatory pathways, contributing to gingivitis. Hormonal Gingivitis Hormonal changes during pregnancy, puberty, or steroid therapy can lead to gingivitis, even in the absence of plaque. For example, pregnancy gingivitis is caused by increased levels of female sex hormones, while puberty-related gingivitis is linked to hormonal receptor activity in gingival tissues. Drug-Induced Gingivitis Certain medications can stimulate fibroblast proliferation or disrupt the balance of extracellular matrix synthesis and degradation, leading to gingival inflammation. Causes The primary cause of gingivitis is inadequate oral hygiene, which allows plaque to form. However, the condition is multifactorial, with contributions from local, systemic, genetic, and behavioral factors. Differentiation from Other Diseases Gingivitis must be distinguished from other conditions that mimic its presentation. Epidemiology and Demographics Gingivitis is the most common periodontal disease, affecting individuals of all ages worldwide. It is present in approximately half of the population by age 4 or 5 and peaks at nearly 100% during puberty. The prevalence decreases slightly after puberty but remains constant into adulthood. Males are more commonly affected than females, likely due to better oral hygiene practices among women. Pregnant women are particularly susceptible to severe forms of gingivitis. The condition is also more prevalent in individuals of lower socioeconomic status. Risk Factors Common risk factors include poor oral hygiene, smoking, stress, nutritional deficiencies, and systemic conditions. Complications If untreated, gingivitis can lead to: Recurrence Periodontitis Gingival or jawbone infections Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG or trench mouth) Acute Necrotizing Ulcerative Gingivitis (ANUG) ANUG is a severe form of gingivitis associated with pain, ulceration, spontaneous bleeding, and halitosis. It is more common in developing countries and is exacerbated by factors such as smoking, stress, poor oral hygiene, and immunodeficiency. Treatment includes debridement, antiseptic rinses, and, in severe cases, antibiotics. Prognosis Gingivitis is easily treatable in its early stages. However, if left untreated, it can progress to periodontitis, leading to bone destruction and tooth loss. Clinical Presentation Gingivitis can present acutely or chronically and may be localized or generalized. Types include: Marginal gingivitis: Inflammation confined to the gingival margin. Papillary gingivitis: Involves the interdental papillae. Diffuse gingivitis: Affects the gingival margin, attached gingiva, and interdental papillae. Symptoms Swollen, shiny, or discolored gums Bleeding during brushing or flossing Receding gumline Mouth sores Itching or discomfort Signs Physical examination reveals erythematous, friable gum tissue and pocket depths greater than 3 mm. Diagnosis Diagnosis is based on clinical evaluation, including probing pocket depths. Radiographs are not typically useful for gingivitis but may help rule out periodontitis. Treatment Treatment involves an interprofessional approach to address the underlying causes and prevent progression. Steps include: 1. Professional cleaning to remove plaque and calculus. 2. Reinforcement of oral hygiene practices, including brushing, flossing, and the use of mouthwash. 3. Addressing modifiable factors, such as replacing faulty dental prostheses or adjusting medications. 4. In severe cases, antibiotics may be prescribed. Proper brushing and flossing techniques. Regular use of antiseptic mouthwash. A balanced diet. Routine dental visits every 6 to 12 months, or more frequently for high-risk individuals. Awareness of personal risk factors, such as age, smoking, and systemic conditions.
